title: In a Newly Drawn District, Black Voters May Get a Representative Who Spent Years Undermining Their Interests
author: Wendi C. Thomas
content:
Not two weeks after the Tennessee legislature carved Memphis into three
congressional districts this spring, in a move designed to eliminate
Democratic representation, Republican state Sen. Brent Taylor made his
electoral expectations clear in a photo posted on social media.

Taylor and U.S. Rep. Tim Burchett, a fellow Republican, sat side by side on
the U.S. Capitol steps. “My friend [Tim Burchett](https://burchett.house.gov/)
showing me the dadgum ropes,” Taylor wrote in a Facebook
[post](https://www.facebook.com/BrentTaylorTN/posts/pfbid02W4jk5Q57NmaCZGmxwugqxt4sx751U3sp2ysK7oeemkFq7Bdu2Ve4pLvDo2C4YZL1l).

On May 7, the same day that the new districts were approved, Taylor had
announced his bid to represent the redrawn Congressional District 9, which for
more than four decades had stood as the state’s sole majority Black district.
During that time, it covered mostly the Memphis area; it now stretches across
half the state and is majority white.

Taylor, 58, already has a track record with many of the voters he is now
seeking to represent in Washington, D. C.: In his nearly four years as a state
senator, he has taken steps to strip authority from local officials elected by
many of those same voters. With the backing of a Republican supermajority,
Taylor, who is white, pushed through half a dozen laws that superseded the
power and priorities of local politicians.

Around the country, state legislatures from both parties [have used preemption
laws](https://www.nlc.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/Restoring-City-Rights-in-
an-Era-of-PreemptionWeb.pdf) to control local governments. That tactic has
been embraced by Republican-dominated statehouses in recent years as a way to
restrict the ability of Democratic-led cities to enact policies state leaders
disagree with, including protections for [civil
rights](https://www.wunc.org/politics/2017-03-23/hb2-how-did-we-get-here),
[public health](https://petrieflom.law.harvard.edu/2020/12/21/covid-public-
health-preemption/) and
[workers](https://academic.oup.com/publius/article/54/1/121/7191231).

Memphis has long struggled with high rates of violent crime that have begun to
fall only in the last couple of years. This is where Taylor focused his
legislative efforts. He led the charge to prohibit judges from considering a
defendant’s ability to pay when making bail decisions. He has tried to oust
Steve Mulroy, the first Democrat elected as Shelby County district attorney in
25 years, and pushed through legislation authorizing the state to review every
decision made by his office. And he co-sponsored a law that voided the Memphis
City Council’s ban on police stops for minor traffic infractions, which had
been passed after the 2023 beating death of Black motorist Tyré Nichols.

The question of how to keep communities safe has drawn divergent political
approaches in Memphis — from Mulroy’s focus on rehabilitation as part of his
effort to lower violent crime, to Taylor’s emphasis on aggressive prosecution
and incarceration. Those approaches can mean very different experiences for
the people of Memphis, which makes up most of Shelby County. Some elected
officials and criminal justice experts warn that the laws Taylor has
championed will embolden police to detain drivers without justification and
the criminal justice system to lock up more people for longer periods in the
already overcrowded county jail, where [more than 65
people](https://www.justcity.org/jail) have died since 2018.

“I think he’s very dangerous for Shelby County, and he’s going to be very
dangerous for the Ninth District if he gets elected,” said former Shelby
County General Sessions Court Judge Bill Anderson, referring to how Taylor’s
policies could especially harm Black men. Anderson retired in May 2025 after
clashing publicly with Taylor over bail reform measures. (Anderson supported
them; Taylor opposed them.)

Taylor is [favored to
win](https://www.realclearpolling.com/polls/house/general/2026/tennessee/district-9/taylor-
vs-pearson) because of redistricting by Tennessee Republicans after a U.S.
Supreme Court ruling in April made it harder to challenge gerrymandering that
dilutes the Black vote. The Mississippi native, who lives in an antebellum-
style mansion in a tiny and heavily white community east of Memphis, has
[loaned his congressional
campaign](https://www.fec.gov/data/candidate/H6TN09464/?tab=summary) $1.5
million. The candidate [made millions after
selling](https://x.com/BrentTaylorTN/status/2013982030455857647) his funeral
home businesses to a private equity firm.

Taylor’s opponent is state Rep. Justin J. Pearson, a 31-year-old Black
Democrat who has taken a very different approach to what the district needs.
Pearson has called for addressing the root causes of crime by improving
schools and economic opportunities instead of a singular focus on
incarceration. He first made national headlines for his role in [stopping the
construction](https://mlk50.com/2021/07/02/byhalia-connection-pipeline-pulls-
project/) of [an oil pipeline](https://mlk50.com/category/environmental-
justice/byhalia-connection-pipeline/) in a Black Memphis neighborhood. He is
also one of two Democratic legislators [expelled by the Republican
supermajority](https://www.npr.org/2023/08/04/1192068281/the-2-expelled-
members-of-the-tennessee-3-win-back-their-state-house-seats) after leading a
protest calling for gun control following a 2023 school shooting. With deep
family roots in southwest Memphis, Pearson has positioned himself as the
better fit for the historically Democratic Ninth Congressional District. He
has also received support from national Democrats and has [outraised Taylor in
campaign
donations](https://www.fec.gov/data/candidate/H6TN09449/?cycle=2026#total-
raised).

![A man wearing a suit speaks to a crowd of people who are holding signs that
say, “Justin Pearson” and “Stop Toxic Data
Centers.”](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/080626_KW_PearsonWatchParty052_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=1149)Democratic
congressional candidate state Rep. Justin J. Pearson speaks to supporters
after an election night watch party for the state’s primaries in Memphis,
Tennessee, in August. Kevin Wurm/MLK50/CatchLight Local/Report for America

Taylor, who declined to be interviewed for this story, has said that the laws
he has championed [prioritize public
safety](https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/aec6b021-9090-675f-f1d1-f3d07f455394/2025-09-30%20-%20Testimony%20-%20Taylor.pdf).
He did not respond to detailed questions.

But John Pfaff, a professor at Fordham School of Law who has [studied how
state preemption laws impact
prosecutors](https://scholarlycommons.law.northwestern.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=7777&context=jclc),
said [tough-on-crime laws](https://www.cnn.com/2016/03/23/politics/john-
ehrlichman-richard-nixon-drug-war-blacks-hippie) like the ones Taylor helped
pass have historically been “a form of social control against disliked
minority groups” under the guise of public safety. **  
****  
**Non-urban voters, Pfaff said, “do feel, however incorrectly, sort of
victimized by expanding civil rights” that urban voters choose. While these
voters cannot cast ballots in city elections, he said, they have another path
by which to exert power: “If the suburbs and rural areas control the
governor’s mansion and the state legislature, they then can use their power
there through preemption laws that finally tell Memphis what they want Memphis
to do.”

### Prohibiting Limits on Police Traffic Stops

In January 2023, the month Taylor took office, the nation was shaken by video
of violent policing in Memphis.  
  
A street surveillance camera and police body cameras captured what happened
after undercover Memphis police officers pulled over 29-year-old Nichols just
a few blocks from his mother’s home. For three minutes, officers repeatedly
punched the unarmed man in the face, hit him with a baton and kicked him as he
screamed for his mom. Nichols would die from his injuries in the hospital
three days later.  
  
After pressure from Nichols’ family and community organizers, the Memphis City
Council unanimously passed an ordinance in April of that year barring police
from pulling motorists over for [minor traffic
violations](https://www.yahoo.com/news/memphis-passes-driving-equality-
ordinance-230733788.html?guccounter=1&guce_referrer=aHR0cHM6Ly93d3cuZ29vZ2xlLmNvbS8&guce_referrer_sig=AQAAAG82b9boAJu_YjPMDAmWE6ZaJ3FKQJvm0B_2Rld-
urB7iyYjlC1rAkImNpsyGinEmyxlTTevhuYkAGtR4-7fRekdVijW8S84HhFxMt7QfdZULzO4C4wNLxNi-
BKBUKyaumb47-6bNSCqY1kq6ZU5CaA_aSjKNmX6J7u_u1qxr763), such as a broken tail
light, as a pretext for investigating an unrelated, more serious crime.
Research shows that these stops are disproportionately used to [detain Black
drivers](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32367028/), [undermine the public’s
trust](https://scholarlycommons.law.case.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=4660&context=caselrev)
in police and create [unnecessary police
encounters](https://review.law.stanford.edu/wp-
content/uploads/sites/3/2024/01/Heydari-76-Stan.-L.-Rev.-1.pdf) that can turn
deadly.

![A woman speaks into numerous microphones. She is in the midst of a crowd of
people outdoors. The other people hold signs that say, “Tyre” and “I am a
man.” Behind them, a large sculpture spells out the words “I am a
man.”](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/250605_TN_Nichols_Bday_BV_0019_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=2560)RowVaughn
Wells, center, with family, friends and supporters during a community rally
and celebration of what would have been Tyré Nichols’ 32nd birthday outside of
the I Am a Man Plaza in Memphis in June 2025. Brad Vest for MLK50

Taylor, who had been in the state Senate for a few months when the city
ordinance passed, said it made the public less safe by limiting the potential
for police to investigate more serious crimes. The next year, he and state
Rep. John Gillespie, a Shelby County Republican, [sponsored legislation that
prohibited](https://wapp.capitol.tn.gov/apps/BillInfo/Default?BillNumber=SB2572&ga=113)
local government from curbing law enforcement’s ability to conduct traffic
stops, effectively undoing Memphis’ ordinance.

Nichols’ mother, RowVaughn Wells, pleaded with lawmakers to drop the bill.
Speaking on the Senate floor, Taylor responded, saying that as a funeral home
director, he empathized with the Nichols’ family, but “we can’t let that
empathy, Mr. Speaker, cloud our judgment in protecting 7 million Tennesseans.”

Taylor’s intervention suggests “that Memphis voters don’t know what their best
interests are,” said Martavius Jones, who was chair of the Memphis City
Council when the city ordinance passed. “What we were trying to do would not
jeopardize the safety of anyone — not even in Memphis, but much less the rest
of the population of Tennessee.”

Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee, a Republican, [told reporters before signing the
law](https://apnews.com/article/tyre-nichols-memphis-tennessee-police-
reforms-343023edc2ed0062f33aa0b540becff6) that no one should limit police in
their enforcement methods and officers should be held accountable for their
actions.

“I think what’s most important for us to remember is that we can give law
enforcement tools,” Lee said, “but we’ve got to hold law enforcement to a
standard of using those tools appropriately, where there’s an appropriate
interaction with the public.”

Eight months after Tennessee lawmakers passed Taylor’s preemption bill, the
U.S. Department of Justice released its [investigation of the Memphis Police
Department](https://www.justice.gov/crt/media/1379096/dl), finding that its
aggressive traffic enforcement had harmed Memphians. The Justice Department
recommended that the city limit the use of pretextual stops. Such police
activity enabled the “regular use of excessive force with impunity” and
unlawfully discriminated against Black residents, the Biden administration’s
report said. When President Donald Trump took office in 2025, his Justice
Department [retracted those findings](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/us-
department-justices-civil-rights-division-dismisses-biden-era-police-
investigations-and).

Over the last year, law enforcement has ramped up the use of such stops,
[especially in immigration
enforcement](https://www.propublica.org/article/memphis-safe-task-force-
immigration-arrests-crime-data), as Trump’s [Memphis Safe Task
Force](https://www.propublica.org/article/memphis-safe-task-force-police-
harassment) — a collection of more than two dozen state and federal law
enforcement agencies, including the National Guard — descended upon the city.
Taylor supported the effort, [testifying before the U.S.
Senate](https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/aec6b021-9090-675f-f1d1-f3d07f455394/2025-09-30%20-%20Testimony%20-%20Taylor.pdf)
days before it began that the task force would “succeed in doing the hard work
to infiltrate gangs and arrest more routine criminals.”

### Unprecedented Scrutiny of a District Attorney

Since his first year in the state Senate, Taylor had also been working to
displace the decision-making authority of another locally elected office:
district attorneys, especially Mulroy, one of Tennessee's two Democratic
county prosecutors. Taylor called him a [“far-left
zealot”](https://www.actionnews5.com/2022/08/22/campaign-letter-republican-
state-senate-candidate-sparks-controversy/?outputType=amp) who “has the
potential to make the scourge of violent crime even worse.”  

![A man holding a microphone gestures with his hand as he speaks. In the
background, a crowd is holding signs that say, “Still Seeking Justice. Tyre
Nichols.”](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/260107-TyreVigil-0257_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=1149)Shelby
County District Attorney Steve Mulroy speaks at a vigil for the third
anniversary of Nichols’ death in Memphis in January. Andrea Morales/MLK50

In 2023, Taylor sponsored a law that transferred the power to review certain
death penalty cases from county prosecutors, who are elected, to the state
attorney general, who is appointed by the state Supreme Court. While the law
applied statewide, it disproportionately impacted Shelby County, where half of
the state’s 40 death row prisoners were prosecuted. The law, Mulroy said at
the time, “[effectively disenfranchises the
voters](https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/TNSHELBYDA/bulletins/35e63ee)”
who chose their district attorney.

Taylor would go on to further weaken Mulroy’s office following Trump’s 2025
deployment of his crime task force to Memphis. As arrests soared, Taylor
worked to place the district attorney’s decisions under unprecedented
scrutiny, saying he [wanted to
ensure](https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/aec6b021-9090-675f-f1d1-f3d07f455394/2025-09-30%20-%20Testimony%20-%20Taylor.pdf)
that the prosecution of task force cases was as aggressive as the task force
itself.

[One new law](https://publications.tnsosfiles.com/acts/114/pub/pc0928.pdf),
co-sponsored by Taylor, authorized the state attorney general to review every
case that comes through Mulroy’s office, including those that stem from
arrests made by Trump’s task force, “to ensure the proper administration of
justice necessary to protect the safety of the community.” The dispositions of
each case, along with bail recommendations, would be reported to legislative
leaders.

Republican state Rep. Andrew Farmer, who introduced the bill in the House,
noted that it is designed to ensure that “all crimes that deserve to be
prosecuted are prosecuted.”

Mulroy is “just going to have to work harder and ensure that people are
continuing to stay safe,” Farmer [said on the House
floor](https://tnga.granicus.com/player/clip/33297?view_id=775&meta_id=974915&redirect=true).
“We want Memphis to continue on the path that it’s going —  up.”

The state’s [district attorneys general conference](https://www.tndagc.org/),
led by Republican former District Attorney Stephen Crump, opposed an early
version of the bill, which would have applied to district attorneys across the
state, because it could lead prosecutors to second-guess their decisions. He
dropped his objections after the bill was narrowed to apply to only Mulroy.

That law has another provision aimed at Mulroy as well: If he declines to
prosecute specific categories of crime, the state attorney general can ask the
state Supreme Court to intervene by installing a temporary district attorney
who would then decide whether to prosecute. Taylor has long sought to[ limit
Mulroy’s authority](https://mlk50.com/2024/07/03/state-sen-taylor-is-seeking-
to-oust-da-mulroy-the-move-is-rooted-in-misinformation/), and the provision
would be a way to do so. Mulroy said the effect would be “an unelected shadow
DA operating in parallel to the duly elected DA.”

“Prosecutorial discretion and prosecutorial independence is a key fundamental
part of our criminal justice system,” Mulroy said. “It’s clear under both the
text of the Tennessee constitution and Tennessee Supreme Court case law, and
this bill does great violence to those principles.”

Taylor [co-sponsored a second
law](https://publications.tnsosfiles.com/acts/114/pub/pc0943.pdf), passed in
May, that requires Mulroy’s office to report to the state and the U.S.
Department of Justice within 10 business days every time it has entered into a
plea deal, or dismissed or lowered the charges on a felony offense that
resulted from a task force arrest.

“Memphis residents deserve confidence that the significant investments being
made to combat violent crime are matched with accountability at every level of
the justice system,” Gillespie, who co-sponsored the bill in the House, [said
at the time](https://tnhousegop.org/press-releases/2026/01/rep-john-gillespie-
aims-to-enhance-transparency-in-memphis-safe-task-force-prosecutions/).

Taylor argued the reporting requirements were necessary to give the federal
government an opportunity to prosecute cases Mulroy dismissed. In [a post on
X](https://x.com/BrentTaylorTN/status/1982175130106335590) and a [statement
made before the U.S. Senate Judiciary
Committee](https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/aec6b021-9090-675f-f1d1-f3d07f455394/2025-09-30%20-%20Testimony%20-%20Taylor.pdf),
he called Mulroy “the weak link” in the task force’s efforts. He’s also
[claimed, without evidence,](https://mlk50.com/2024/07/03/state-sen-taylor-is-
seeking-to-oust-da-mulroy-the-move-is-rooted-in-misinformation/) that Mulroy
refuses to prosecute crimes.  
  
In a rebuttal, Mulroy [noted that more than 40,000
defendants](https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/TNSHELBYDA/bulletins/4134964)
are prosecuted by his office each year.  
  
Mulroy has [sued to stop both laws](https://www.scdag.com/news-
releases/shelby-county-da-files-lawsuit-challenging-new-state-oversight-laws),
claiming they are unconstitutional because they unfairly single out Shelby
County and create an administrative burden. [The
lawsuit](https://washingtonlitigationgroup.org/press-release/wlg-files-suit-
on-behalf-of-shelby-county-district-attorney-steven-mulroy/) is pending in
state court. Meanwhile, Mulroy has objected to his staff spending time on the
reporting requirements, which he called “[pointless
busywork](https://www.scdag.com/news-releases/shelby-county-da-files-lawsuit-
challenging-new-state-oversight-laws).”

Mulroy’s election in 2022 as the county’s first Democratic district attorney
in more than two decades came on the heels of a year with a record number of
homicides. But Republicans’ tough-on-crime approach had grown unpopular with
voters, and Mulroy vowed to be an alternative. He [promised to
deprioritize](https://www.aclu-tn.org/steve-mulroy-candidate-questionnaire-
responses/) the prosecution of low-level offenses such as marijuana possession
and shoplifting; emphasize rehabilitation such as drug treatment, mental
health counseling and job training; and establish a unit to examine the
validity of convictions.

One of the people who campaigned for him was William Arnold, who had spent
nearly seven years in state prison before his [conviction was
dismissed](https://www.newschannel5.com/news/charges-dropped-against-
nashville-mentor-after-nearly-seven-years-in-jail) following examination by a
Davidson County [conviction review unit](https://da.nashville.gov/wp-
content/uploads/2017/05/RJ-1.pdf). The community organizer said he saw
Mulroy’s candidacy as a way to “support someone who could help Memphians in a
different way.”

To see Mulroy’s power being muted by Taylor is disheartening, Arnold said. But
that is not surprising to him, given how the state legislature has long
treated the predominantly Black city, including [replacing the Memphis Shelby
County Schools’ elected
board](https://www.chalkbeat.org/tennessee/2026/05/26/tennessee-republicans-
appoint-memphis-state-takeover-board/) with a state-appointed one.

![A close-up photo of a man with a serious
expression.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/William_Arnold_02-scaled_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=1149)William
Arnold, who spent nearly seven years incarcerated for a crime he did not
commit, is now a community organizer and a supporter of Mulroy. Brandon Dill
for MLK50

### Bail Calculator Scrapped

Among the preemptive legislation Taylor has sponsored, a 2023 effort stood
out: the dismantling of a bipartisan effort to ensure Shelby County’s bail
practices did not discriminate against poor people, who are disproportionately
Black.  
  
Under state law, magistrates are to “impose the [least onerous
conditions”](https://law.justia.com/codes/tennessee/2021/title-40/chapter-11/part-1/section-40-11-116/)
when deciding bail and should set bail “[as low as the
court](https://law.justia.com/codes/tennessee/2021/title-40/chapter-11/part-1/section-40-11-118/)
determines is necessary” to assure the defendant returns to court.  
  
But in practice, hundreds of people were being detained at the Shelby County
Jail simply because they couldn’t afford bail, [according to Just
City](https://www.justcity.org/), a Memphis criminal justice reform
organization, which along with the American Civil Liberties Union [threatened
to sue the county](https://www.aclu-tn.org/app/uploads/2021/12/Shelby-County-
Demand-Letter.pdf) in 2021 for violating existing state law. Being jailed
while awaiting trial can cause arrestees to lose jobs and child custody, the
organizations argued.

In August 2022, the organizations and county officials — including Mulroy’s
predecessor, Republican District Attorney Amy Weirich — [agreed on a new bail
order](https://mlk50.com/2022/08/25/aclu-other-advocates-land-bail-policy-
they-wanted-in-shelby-county/) that included an “ability to pay” calculator.

That tool quickly drew Taylor’s ire, and by the following January he had [co-
sponsored a
bill](https://wapp.capitol.tn.gov/apps/BillInfo/Default?BillNumber=SB2565&ga=113)
to kill it, characterizing the calculator in a [Senate Judiciary
Committee](https://tnga.granicus.com/player/clip/30094?view_id=703&meta_id=819097&redirect=true)
meeting as a way of “essentially asking defendants how much money they happen
to have in their pocket so that they can make bail.”

The bill’s supporters said judges should prioritize public safety when
deciding whether to release defendants. “There is blood running in the streets
of Memphis today because they’re letting people out,” state Rep. William
Lamberth, a Republican, said on the House floor.

State law requires judges, when setting bail, to consider several factors,
including a defendant’s financial condition. And Josh Spickler, executive
director of Just City, said that’s exactly what the tool helped judges do.

Under Taylor’s law, however, “the defendant’s ability to pay shall not be
considered.”

“That tied our hands as judges,” Anderson, the former Shelby County judge,
said in an interview.

A 2025 [University of Memphis
study](https://www.memphis.edu/ccre/pretrial_ccre_commission_20250326.pdf)
found that the median bail amount increased after Taylor’s law took effect.
And the law’s impact falls [hardest on Black
residents](https://datacollaborativeforjustice.org/wp-
content/uploads/2023/02/DisparitiesReport-27.pdf), Anderson said, because they
are more likely to be low-income and make up a disproportionate share of
Shelby County jail occupants.

“To those of us in the system, it’s obvious what he’s doing,” said Anderson,
who resigned in 2025 with six years left of his eight-year term. “He called
them reform acts, but they’re not reform.”

Spent Years Undermining Their
Interests](https://www.propublica.org/article/brent-taylor-memphis-tennessee-
preemption-laws) appeared first on [ProPublica](https://www.propublica.org).
